stem: Which table problem is an accidental duplicate?

options.text: The same event was imported twice with identical identifying details
One customer legitimately bought twice
Two people share an age
A column contains numbers

explanation_after: A duplicate repeats the same real record because of collection or import trouble. Two genuine events can look similar without being duplicates.

stem: Why is mixing kilograms and grams in one numeric column dangerous?

options.text: The model treats the numbers as one scale and may learn a false pattern
Models cannot read any numbers
Units matter only when printing
It automatically removes every row

explanation_after: A value of 5 kilograms and 5000 grams describe the same weight but look vastly different. Standardizing units makes the numbers comparable.

stem: When should an imputer learn its replacement value?

options.text: After splitting, from training rows only
From the full table before splitting
From test answers only
After production predictions are returned

explanation_after: Learning the replacement from all rows lets held-out data influence training. Fit the imputer on training rows and reuse its saved value later.

stem: A new supplier sends birth years in a column that used to contain ages. Which check catches this best?

options.text: An allowed range and unit rule in the data contract
Checking that every value is numeric
Sorting the rows alphabetically
Changing the model name

explanation_after: Both ages and birth years are numbers, so type checking alone passes them. A range and unit rule describes what the numbers are supposed to mean.

stem: Why might adding a “was missing” flag help a model?

options.text: The fact that a value is absent may itself carry useful information
It guarantees every guessed value is correct
It removes the need to inspect missingness
It converts all columns to text

explanation_after: Sometimes missingness follows a real pattern. The flag lets the model use that pattern separately from the filled numeric value.

stem: A field is often missing because people with unusually high values avoid answering. Why can filling every blank with the average be misleading?

options.text: The missing group is systematically different, so the average hides the pattern and pulls estimates downward
Averages are never numbers
Every blank happened by pure accident
The model will refuse all complete rows

explanation_after: The blanks are linked to the hidden value itself. Replacing them with an ordinary average makes that special group look typical and can bias conclusions.

options.text: Apply the saved cleaning rules to test rows
Split rows into training and test groups
Fit the cleaning rules on training rows
Train the model on cleaned training rows

explanation_after: Split first, learn cleaning rules from training rows, train on the cleaned training data, and only then apply the saved rules to held-out rows.

prompt: Choose the chip: `imputer.____(X_train)` should learn replacement values from training rows.

options.text: fit
predict
score
delete

explanation_after: `fit` learns and stores the replacement values. Later, `transform` applies those saved values without learning from held-out rows.
